## 📐 Section 1 — Data preparation (1 point)

Load your series and put it on a regular time grid.

- Resolve duplicated timestamps if there are any, and say in one sentence what you decided
  and why.
- Fill the calendar so gaps become visible missing values rather than absent rows.
- State the frequency, the span, and how many complete seasonal cycles you have.

You did all of this in Week 1. It should take ten minutes.

::: {.callout-warning collapse="false"}
## ⚠️ Where this goes wrong: the frequency string

- `"W"` does not mean "weekly". It means *week ending Sunday*. If your timestamps are
  Mondays, a grid built with `"W"` lines up with nothing and your series comes back empty.
  Use the anchored form, `"W-MON"` — which is what `spec["freq"]` already gives you.
- pandas 3 removed the bare `"M"`, `"Q"`, `"Y"` and `"H"` aliases. Use `"MS"`/`"ME"`,
  `"QS"`/`"QE"`, `"YS"`/`"YE"` and lowercase `"h"`. A bare `"Q"` now raises rather than warns.
- `"MS"` is month **start**, `"ME"` is month **end**. Pick the one your timestamps already
  use, or every row misses the grid by a few days.

After building a grid, check that you did not lose everything:
`s["y"].notna().sum()` should be close to the number of rows you started with.

📖 [offset aliases](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/user_guide/timeseries.html#offset-aliases) · [anchored offsets](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/user_guide/timeseries.html#anchored-offsets) ·
[`date_range`](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.date_range.html) · [`reindex`](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.reindex.html) ·
[`duplicated`](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.Series.duplicated.html) · [`interpolate`](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.Series.interpolate.html)
:::


## 📊 Section 2 — EDA and visualisation (4 points)

This is the heaviest section. Four plots and two decompositions, each with a sentence
saying what you see — a plot with no reading attached earns nothing.

**Graphics.** Time plot, seasonal plot, seasonal subseries plot, ACF. Name the patterns:
trend, seasonality, cycles, level shifts, outliers.

::: {.callout-warning collapse="false"}
## ⚠️ Where this goes wrong

- `plot_acf` raises once `lags` reaches the length of the series. Keep it well below —
  `lags=min(40, len(y) // 3)` is a safe default, and for weekly data you want at least
  `lags=60` to see the annual spike.
- Plot the ACF of the series **with missing values removed**; `plot_acf` will not handle
  `NaN` for you.

📖 [`plot_acf`](https://www.statsmodels.org/stable/generated/statsmodels.graphics.tsaplots.plot_acf.html)
:::


**Variance.** Does the size of the seasonal swing grow with the level of the series? If it
does, the additive decompositions below are the wrong model for it.

- Estimate a Box-Cox $\lambda$ (`boxcox_lambda` from `coreforecast`, as in the lecture).
- Plot the transformed series next to the original.
- **Decide** whether to work transformed or untransformed, and justify the decision in a
  sentence. A defensible "no transformation needed" is worth full marks; an unexplained
  transformation is not.

📖 [`boxcox` / `boxcox_lambda`](https://nixtlaverse.nixtla.io/coreforecast/) · [`scipy.stats.boxcox`](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/generated/scipy.stats.boxcox.html, an
alternative that returns the transform and λ together) · [FPP 3.1 transformations](https://otexts.com/fpp3/transformations.html) ·
[FPP the Pythonic Way, ch. 3](https://otexts.com/fpppy/nbs/03-decomposition.html)


::: {.callout-warning}
## If your series contains zeros

`boxcox_lambda(..., method="loglik")` refuses non-positive values outright. `method="guerrero"`
accepts them but may return $\lambda = 0$, which *is* the log transform — undefined at zero.
A multiplicative decomposition refuses them for the same reason.

That is information about your series, not an obstacle. Find out where the zeros come from
before deciding what to do about them, and say what you concluded. This is exactly the kind
of judgement the point is for.
:::

**Decomposition.** Two of them, on whichever version of the series you settled on:

- classical decomposition (`seasonal_decompose`);
- STL (`STL`), with a stated choice of `seasonal` and `robust`.

Then compare them. Where do they disagree, and which do you trust more on this series?

::: {.callout-warning collapse="false"}
## ⚠️ Where this goes wrong

- `seasonal_decompose` returns `NaN` for the first and last `period / 2` observations —
  six months at each end of a monthly series. That is the centred moving average, not a
  bug, and it is one of the differences you are asked to comment on.
- `model="multiplicative"` refuses zeros and negative values outright.
- `STL(...)` needs `seasonal` to be an **odd** integer ≥ 3, and it must be an `int`, not a
  float. `robust=True` costs a little accuracy and buys resistance to outliers.
- Both need `period` — the number of observations in one cycle, which is `mine["season"]`,
  not the number of years.

📖 [`seasonal_decompose`](https://www.statsmodels.org/stable/generated/statsmodels.tsa.seasonal.seasonal_decompose.html) · [`STL`](https://www.statsmodels.org/stable/generated/statsmodels.tsa.seasonal.STL.html) ·
[FPP 3.4 classical decomposition](https://otexts.com/fpp3/classical-decomposition.html) · [FPP 3.6 STL](https://otexts.com/fpp3/stl.html)
:::


::: {.callout-note}
## What "reading the components" means

Not "the trend goes up". Something a colleague could act on: *the seasonal component is
stable until 2008 and shifts afterwards*, *the remainder is flat except for three spikes
which line up with the crisis*, *the trend flattens in the last two years*.
:::

## 🔢 Section 3 — Implementation (2 points)

**Strength of components.** Compute, from the STL fit:

$$
F_T = \max\left(0,\; 1 - \frac{\operatorname{Var}(R_t)}{\operatorname{Var}(T_t + R_t)}\right)
\qquad
F_S = \max\left(0,\; 1 - \frac{\operatorname{Var}(R_t)}{\operatorname{Var}(S_t + R_t)}\right)
$$

Report both, rounded to two decimals.

📖 [FPP 4.3 — where $F_T$ and $F_S$ come from](https://otexts.com/fpp3/stlfeatures.html)

Both come out of a **fitted** STL object: `fit.trend`, `fit.seasonal`, `fit.resid`. If you
get a value outside $[0, 1]$, you have almost certainly passed the STL object instead of
the result of `.fit()`.


**Seasonally adjusted series.** Produce and plot it. Say what it is useful for and what it
hides.

**Explaining last week's winner.** In Lab 2 you found which simple method won on your
series. Now explain **why**, with the decomposition.

- Set `LAB2_WINNER` to the method that won in your Lab 2 — it is in your
  `SURNAME_lab02_summary.csv`.
- In three or four sentences, explain that result using $F_T$, $F_S$ and what the components
  show: which component carries the variance, and what the winning method copies forward
  that the other three do not.
- If your Lab 2 prediction was wrong, say what the decomposition shows that the plots did not.

::: {.callout-important}
Marked on the **reasoning**. "snaive won because snaive usually wins" scores nothing, even
though it is usually true.
:::
